q: Every controller up to week 5 read qpos[:7]. Why does the course call that 'cheating'?
choices: It is the pelvis position and orientation, which no G1 sensor measures
It is the joint angles, which the real G1 must estimate from torque
It is the previous action, which a policy is not allowed to see
It is the raw IMU reading, before the noise is added in software
why: qpos[:7] is the floating base: 3 position numbers plus a quaternion. There is no sensor for 'where am I in the room', so it is privileged; the joint angles are qpos[7:].

q: Which sensors does the G1 actually have?
choices: Two IMUs and joint encoders, nothing else
Two IMUs, foot contact switches and encoders
A head camera, one IMU and joint torque sensors
One IMU, a magnetometer and joint encoders
why: Torso and pelvis IMUs (each a gyro plus accelerometer) and the joint encoders. No cameras, no torque sensors, no foot contact switches.

q: Which part of qpos may a controller for the real G1 fairly use?
choices: qpos[7:], the joint angles, read by encoders
qpos[:7], the pelvis pose, read by the IMU
qpos[:3], the pelvis position, from the accelerometer
None of it; only qvel can be measured
why: A real robot reads its own joint angles, so qpos[7:] is fair. The pelvis pose qpos[:7] is not measured by anything: the IMU gives rates and specific force, not pose.

q: How many sensor numbers per timestep do the G1's two IMUs provide?
choices: 12: a gyro and an accelerometer, 3 axes each, twice
6: one gyro and one accelerometer, 3 axes each
4: one number per sensor, since nsensor = 4
29: one per actuated joint of the robot
why: nsensor = 4 is four 3-axis sensors (gyro + accelerometer at torso and at pelvis), 12 numbers per step. 29 is the number of actuators.

q: Two identical G1 runs give identical sensordata, although the MJCF declares noise. What does the course conclude?
choices: 'Convenient and dishonest': inject noise and bias by hand
The sensors are ideal, so test estimators on them as they are
Noise is applied only on Colab, so test there instead
Declared noise appears only once the robot starts walking
why: This MuJoCo build applies no sensor noise, so readings are exactly deterministic. An estimator tested on perfect sensors teaches nothing, so noise and gyro bias are added by hand.

q: Proof mass on a spring: m·a = f_spring + m·g. The chip reads only the spring. So it reports…
choices: The specific force f = a − g
The true acceleration a of the body
Gravity alone, g, in body axes
The sum a + g of motion and gravity
why: Solving for the spring force per kilogram gives f = a − g: every force except gravity, per kilogram. That is why 'the accelerometer does not measure acceleration'.

q: In the body's own axes (R maps body to world), the accelerometer reads…
choices: f_b = Rᵀ(a − g)
f_b = R(a − g)
f_b = Rᵀ(a + g)
f_b = Rᵀa − g
why: The chip is bolted to the body, so a world vector is seen in body axes as Rᵀ times it, and the vector is the specific force a − g. Rotating with R instead of Rᵀ goes the wrong way.

q: What does an accelerometer on a robot standing perfectly still read?
choices: 9.81 m/s² pointing up, in its own axes
Zero, because the robot is not accelerating
9.81 m/s² pointing down, along gravity
Zero vertically and 9.81 along its x axis
why: At rest a = 0, so f = a − g = −g: 9.81 m/s² UP. 'Reads zero at rest' is the guide's named trap; zero is the free-fall reading.

q: Practice Q16: an accelerometer at rest reads (0, 0, 9.81). The robot is dropped. What does it read during the fall?
choices: (0, 0, 9.81), unchanged
why: In free fall a = g, so f = a − g = 0: nothing touches the proof mass. It does not keep reading 9.81, and it does not flip sign.

q: A lift accelerates upward at 2 m/s² (g ≈ 9.81). What does an accelerometer on its floor read vertically?
choices: About 11.8 m/s² up
About 7.8 m/s² up
About 2 m/s² up
About 9.8 m/s² up
why: f = a − g = 2 − (−9.81) = 11.81 m/s² up: more than at rest, because the floor pushes harder. 7.8 is the lift accelerating downward.

q: A lift accelerates downward at 2 m/s². What does the accelerometer read vertically?
choices: About 7.8 m/s² up
About 11.8 m/s² up
About 2 m/s² down
Zero
why: f = a − g = −2 − (−9.81) = 7.81 m/s² up: less than at rest, but not zero (that needs full free fall, a = g).

q: 'An accelerometer reads zero in free fall.' Is that right?
choices: Yes: a = g, so a − g = 0
No: it reads 9.81 m/s² down
No: it reads 9.81 m/s² up, as at rest
No: it reads 19.62 m/s², twice g
why: The guide: 'zero at rest' is wrong, 'zero in free fall' is right. Falling, the case and the proof mass accelerate together and the spring is unloaded.

q: Why is an accelerometer a tilt sensor?
choices: At rest its reading points 'up', written in the body's axes
It integrates its turning rate into an angle over time
It measures the body's own acceleration, which tilt causes
Its proof mass swings like a pendulum toward the floor
why: At rest f = −g, so the reading's direction is 'up' expressed in body axes; tilt the body and 'up' moves among those axes. Integrating a rate is the gyro's job.

q: At rest, the roll angle from the accelerometer is…
choices: φ = atan2(f_y, f_z)
φ = atan2(f_z, f_y)
φ = atan2(−f_x, f_z)
φ = asin(f_y), taking g = 1
why: At rest f_b = g(−sin θ, sin φ cos θ, cos φ cos θ), so f_y/f_z = tan φ. The argument order is atan2(y, x); −f_x belongs to pitch.

q: At rest, the pitch angle from the accelerometer is…
choices: θ = atan2(−f_x, √(f_y² + f_z²))
θ = atan2(f_x, f_z)
θ = atan2(f_y, √(f_x² + f_z²))
θ = atan2(−f_x, f_y + f_z)
why: f_x = −g sin θ and √(f_y² + f_z²) = g cos θ, so their ratio gives tan θ. The y and z parts combine as a root of squares, not a sum.

q: Why does the value of g not matter in the accelerometer tilt formulas?
choices: It cancels in the ratio: only the reading's direction matters
It is fixed at 9.81 everywhere, so it is a known constant
The chip divides every reading by g before reporting it
It does matter: g must be known to 1 % for 1° accuracy
why: Both atan2 arguments carry the same factor g, which cancels. So the estimate uses the direction of f, not its magnitude.

q: At rest the accelerometer reads f = (0, 4.9, 8.5) m/s². What is the roll?
choices: About 30°
About 60°
About 0°
About 45°
why: φ = atan2(4.9, 8.5): tan φ ≈ 0.58, so φ ≈ 30° (sin 30° · 9.81 = 4.9, cos 30° · 9.81 = 8.5). 60° comes from swapping the arguments.

q: At rest the accelerometer reads f = (−4.9, 0, 8.5) m/s². What is the pitch?
choices: About +30°
About −30°
About +60°
About 0°
why: θ = atan2(−f_x, √(f_y² + f_z²)) = atan2(4.9, 8.5) ≈ +30°. Forgetting the minus sign on f_x gives −30°.

q: Why can no accelerometer reading ever contain heading (yaw)?
choices: Turning about the vertical leaves 'up' unchanged: R_z(ψ)ᵀe_z = e_z
Yaw changes only the reading's sign, which atan2 then throws away
Yaw is buried in sensor noise; a better chip would recover it
Yaw shows up only while moving, and the formula assumes rest
why: At rest the reading is g·Rᵀe_z, and the yaw rotation leaves e_z untouched, so ψ drops out of the equation entirely. No amount of precision recovers what is not in the signal.

q: Practice Q19: is the robot's heading (yaw) observable from the IMU alone?
choices: No: gravity is blind to it, and the gyro's integral drifts
Yes: atan2(f_x, f_y) of the accelerometer gives it
Yes: integrating the gyro's ω_z gives it exactly
Only while standing still, when the accelerometer is clean
why: The accelerometer cannot see rotation about the vertical at all, and the gyro gives only a rate whose integral grows as b·t. So yaw is privileged; a magnetometer could help but is unreliable near motors indoors.

q: A box is held still with the same roll and pitch at yaw 0°, 45° and 170°. What are the three accelerometer readings?
choices: Identical
Rotated by 0°, 45° and 170° in the x–y plane
Same direction, scaled by cos(yaw)
Identical in z, with x and y flipped at 170°
why: Measured in the deck: the rows that differ only in yaw give the same reading, which is Step 3 of the derivation (yaw drops out).

q: Why do locomotion policies observe gravity in the body frame rather than the full orientation?
choices: It is the largest piece of attitude a real robot can honestly know
It is cheaper for the network to read than a 4-number quaternion
It contains the heading (yaw) that the policy needs in order to steer
It is exact on hardware, so no filter is ever needed to produce it
why: Roll and pitch are recoverable (gravity plus a filter); yaw is not. So the honest observation is the gravity direction in body axes. On hardware it comes from a filter, with errors.

q: While the robot walks, why does the accelerometer's tilt estimate go wrong?
choices: Sideways acceleration adds into f_y, and atan2 can't tell it from gravity
The gyro bias leaks into the accelerometer through the shared IMU chip
The robot's yaw changes as it walks, rotating the gravity reading
Its noise is far larger than the true tilt signal, even standing
why: The tilt formula assumed a = 0. Walking, f = a − g picks up the body's own acceleration, and every footfall kicks it (|f| ranged 3.4–19.3 m/s²). Yaw does not enter the reading at all.

q: About how much false roll does 1 m/s² of sideways acceleration produce in the accelerometer tilt?
choices: About 5.8°
About 0.1°
About 45°
About 1°
why: atan(1/9.81) ≈ 0.10 rad ≈ 5.8°. 0.1 is the angle in radians, not degrees; 45° would need a sideways acceleration equal to g.

q: An upright robot accelerates sideways at 2 m/s² (take g ≈ 10). Using the small-angle approximation, what false roll does the accelerometer report?
choices: About 0.2 rad, ≈ 11.5°
About 0.02 rad, ≈ 1.1°
About 2 rad, ≈ 115°
About 0.5 rad, ≈ 29°
why: atan(a/g) ≈ a/g = 2/10 = 0.2 rad, and 0.2 × 57.3 ≈ 11.5°. Every 1 m/s² is about 5.8°, so 2 m/s² is about 11.5°.

q: During the G1 walk, over what range did the accelerometer magnitude |f| swing?
why: At rest |f| would be 9.81; walking it strayed up to about 9.5 m/s² either way, from 3.4 to 19.3. That is the footfall kicking the sensor.

q: A gyro reads ω_k = φ̇_k + b. Integrating it for an angle, how does the error grow?
choices: e(t) = b·t: linearly, for ever
e(t) = ½·b·t²: as a parabola
e(t) = b: a constant offset
e(t) ≈ τ·b: bounded
why: Each step adds b·Δt to the error and nothing pulls it back, because the gyro never sees 'up'. ½bt² is double integration of an accelerometer bias; τ·b is the filtered case.

q: A gyro has a bias of 0.01 rad/s. After one minute of integration, how far off is the angle?
choices: 0.6 rad, about 34°
0.6 rad, about 0.6°
18 rad, about 1030°
0.01 rad, about 0.57°
why: e = b·t = 0.01 × 60 = 0.6 rad ≈ 34° (0.57°/s for 60 s). 18 rad is ½bt², the double-integration formula, wrongly applied.

q: Practice Q17: a gyro has bias 0.02 rad/s. Roughly how far off is the integrated angle after 10 s?
choices: About 11.5°, and growing
About 0.2°, and growing
About 57°, and growing
About 1.1°, then bounded
why: b·t = 0.02 × 10 = 0.2 rad, and 0.2 × 57.3 ≈ 11.5°. Forgetting the radian-to-degree conversion gives '0.2°'; a lone gyro is never bounded.

q: A gyro bias of 0.005 rad/s is integrated for 100 s. What is the angle error?
choices: About 29°
About 0.5°
About 1430°
About 2.9°
why: 0.005 × 100 = 0.5 rad ≈ 29°. 1430° is ½bt² (25 rad); 0.5° forgets that the answer is in radians.

q: 'A gyro is right now and wrong later; the accelerometer is the opposite.' What is this describing?
choices: Complementary failure modes of the two sensors
The gyro being noisier than the accelerometer
The accelerometer lagging behind the gyro in time
The torso and pelvis IMUs disagreeing by 0.7°
why: The gyro's error starts tiny and grows as b·t; the accelerometer's is large at every footfall but never grows. Each covers the other's weakness, which is what the filter exploits.

q: Which description fits the accelerometer used as a tilt sensor on a walking robot?
choices: Error large now (every footfall), never grows
Error tiny now (smooth), but grows as b·t
Error large now (footfalls), grows as ½·b·t²
Error tiny now (smooth), and never grows
why: It always sees gravity (so no drift) plus the body's acceleration (so footfall spikes). 'Tiny now, grows as b·t' is the gyro.

q: A constant bias b in measured acceleration is integrated twice for position. The position error grows as…
choices: ½·b·t², a parabola
b·t, a straight line
b·t², with no half
τ·b, bounded
why: Once: velocity error ∫b dt = b·t. Twice: ∫b·s ds = ½bt². Dropping the ½ is the usual slip.

q: An accelerometer bias of 0.01 m/s² is double-integrated for 20 s of standing still. Position error?
choices: 2 m
4 m
why: ½·b·t² = 0.5 × 0.01 × 400 = 2 m. 0.2 m is the velocity-style b·t; 4 m is bt² without the ½.

q: A bias of 0.1 m/s² is double-integrated for 10 s. Position error?
choices: 5 m
1 m
why: ½ × 0.1 × 10² = 5 m. 10 m forgets the ½; 1 m is b·t, the velocity error in m/s mistaken for position.

q: Why is gravity itself the worst accelerometer bias for double integration?
choices: A tilt error δ leaves g·sin δ of gravity uncancelled as fake acceleration
Gravity varies with height, so the bias drifts as the robot moves
The chip cannot measure gravity at all, so it has to be guessed
Gravity adds random noise, not bias, which grows as the square root of t
why: To subtract g you need R, i.e. the tilt. Get it wrong by δ and g·sin δ is left over: 1° leaves about 0.17 m/s², far bigger than a typical chip bias.

q: A 1° tilt error leaves g·sin 1° ≈ 0.17 m/s² uncancelled while the robot stands still. Position error after 10 s and after 20 s?
choices: About 8.6 m and 34 m
About 1.7 m and 3.4 m
About 17 m and 68 m
About 0.86 m and 1.7 m
why: ½ × 0.17 × 100 ≈ 8.6 m, and ½ × 0.17 × 400 ≈ 34 m: doubling t quadruples the error. 1.7/3.4 m is b·t; 17/68 m drops the ½.

q: To know where the G1 is in the room, a student double-integrates its accelerometer. Verdict?
choices: It diverges as ½bt²; position needs a sensor that sees the world
It works once the accelerometer is filtered with α ≈ 0.998
It works while walking, since footfall kicks average out
It works for about an hour, and then needs one reset
why: Any bias (gravity from a 1° tilt is enough) grows as a parabola: 34 m after 20 s of standing. Cameras, GPS or contact with known ground are needed; the G1 has none, so position is privileged.

q: Which is the complementary filter's update?
choices: θ̂_k = α(θ̂_{k−1} + ω_k·Δt) + (1 − α)·θ_acc,k
θ̂_k = α·θ_acc,k + (1 − α)(θ̂_{k−1} + ω_k·Δt)
θ̂_k = α(θ̂_{k−1} + θ_acc,k·Δt) + (1 − α)·ω_k
θ̂_k = θ̂_{k−1} + α·ω_k·Δt + (1 − α)·θ_acc,k
why: Predict with the gyro (θ̂_{k−1} + ω_k·Δt), then blend in a small share (1 − α) of the accelerometer angle. The swapped version puts the big weight α on the accelerometer.

q: In words, what does the complementary filter do?
choices: Trust the gyro over short intervals; let gravity correct it slowly
Trust the accelerometer over short intervals; let the gyro correct it
Average the gyro and accelerometer angles with equal weights
Use the gyro while walking and the accelerometer while standing
why: The gyro is right now and wrong later, the accelerometer the opposite, so the gyro handles fast changes and gravity slowly removes its drift. Equal weighting would let every footfall straight in.

q: What do α = 1 and α = 0 turn the complementary filter into?
choices: A pure gyro (drifts) and a pure accelerometer (kicked every step)
A pure accelerometer (kicked) and a pure gyro (drifts)
A filter frozen at its start value, and an exact copy of the truth
The best filter for standing, and the best filter for walking
why: With α = 1 the accelerometer term vanishes and the gyro is integrated alone; with α = 0 only θ_acc remains. Neither extreme is useful on a walk.

q: At α = 0.995, why does a footfall spike lasting a few ticks barely move the estimate?
choices: Each tick moves only 0.5 % of the way toward the accelerometer angle
Each tick moves 99.5 % of the way toward the accelerometer angle
The gyro detects the spike and the filter rejects that sample
The second (pelvis) IMU averages out the torso IMU's spike
why: 1 − α = 0.005, so a brief kick contributes almost nothing, while a bias that pushes the same way for seconds is steadily pulled back. The filter has no spike detector.

q: As transfer functions, the complementary filter's estimate is…
choices: A low-pass of the accelerometer angle plus a high-pass of the gyro angle
A high-pass of the accelerometer angle plus a low-pass of the gyro angle
A low-pass of both angles, averaged together with the weight α
A band-pass of the gyro rate, centred on the stride frequency
why: L = (1 − α)/(1 − αz⁻¹) passes slow signals (the accelerometer's trustworthy part); H = 1 − L passes fast ones (the gyro's trustworthy part) and blocks its constant bias.

q: The filter's two paths satisfy L(z) + H(z) = 1. What does that guarantee?
choices: With perfect sensors, the estimate equals the true angle
The estimate's error always stays below one degree
The filter is stable for any α, including α > 1
The gyro bias is removed exactly, not merely bounded
why: If both sensors were exact, θ̂ = L·θ + H·θ = θ. It says nothing about error size with real sensors, and the bias is only bounded (≈ τ·b), not removed.

q: What is the complementary filter's time constant τ?
choices: τ = −Δt/ln α ≈ Δt/(1 − α)
τ = Δt·(1 − α)
τ = −ln α/Δt ≈ (1 − α)/Δt
τ = α·Δt/(1 + α)
why: The low-pass memory decays as α^k = e^(k ln α) = e^(−t/τ) with k = t/Δt, so τ = −Δt/ln α, and ln α ≈ α − 1 near 1. Multiplying by (1 − α) instead of dividing is the classic slip.

q: Practice Q18: with Δt = 0.001 s and α = 0.999, what is τ?
choices: About 1 s
About 1 µs
About 0.001 s
About 1000 s
why: τ ≈ Δt/(1 − α) = 0.001/0.001 = 1 s. Δt·(1 − α) would give 10⁻⁶ s, which is the slip.

q: Δt = 0.002 s (500 Hz) and α = 0.998. What is τ?
choices: About 1 s
About 0.5 s
About 0.002 s
About 4 µs
why: 0.002/(1 − 0.998) = 0.002/0.002 = 1 s, the optimum on the course's walk. 4 µs is Δt·(1 − α).

q: Δt = 0.01 s (100 Hz) and α = 0.99. What is τ?
choices: About 1 s
About 0.1 s
About 100 s
About 0.0001 s
why: 0.01/0.01 = 1 s. The same τ can come from different (Δt, α) pairs: α must change with the sample rate to keep the same memory.

q: Δt = 0.002 s and α = 0.99. What is τ?
choices: About 0.2 s
About 2 s
About 0.02 s
About 20 µs
why: 0.002/0.01 = 0.2 s. A smaller α means a shorter memory: more trust in the accelerometer.

q: At Δt = 0.002 s and α = 0.995, what are τ and the crossover frequency f_c?
choices: τ ≈ 4 s, f_c ≈ 0.04 Hz
why: τ ≈ 0.002/0.005 = 0.4 s and f_c = 1/(2πτ) ≈ 0.4 Hz. 2.5 Hz is 1/τ without the 2π.

q: A complementary filter has τ = 1 s. What is its crossover frequency f_c?
choices: About 0.16 Hz
About 1 Hz
About 6.3 Hz
About 0.5 Hz
why: f_c = 1/(2πτ) = 1/6.28 ≈ 0.16 Hz. 1 Hz forgets the 2π; 6.3 Hz multiplies by it.

q: Below and above the crossover frequency f_c, which sensor's angle does the filter follow?
choices: Below f_c the accelerometer; above it the gyro
Below f_c the gyro; above it the accelerometer
The gyro at every frequency once α > 0.99
The accelerometer at every frequency while standing
why: The accelerometer goes through the low-pass (slow trends, gravity), the gyro through the high-pass (fast motion). That is why the bias (0 Hz) is removed and footfalls (0.77 Hz and up) are cut.

q: What does a gyro bias b cost inside the complementary filter, compared with integrating the gyro alone?
choices: A bounded error, e_∞ ≈ τ·b, instead of b·t
Still b·t, but slower by a factor α
Nothing: the high-pass removes it exactly
A bounded error, e_∞ ≈ b/τ, smaller for larger τ
why: Standing still, the error settles at α·Δt·b/(1 − α) ≈ τ·b. 'Trust the gyro for τ seconds and you inherit τ seconds' worth of its bias, never more.' Larger τ means MORE bias error, not less.

q: A filter with τ = 1 s runs on a gyro biased by 0.01 rad/s. What is the steady error?
choices: About 0.01 rad, ≈ 0.57°
About 0.6 rad, ≈ 34°
About 1 rad, ≈ 57°
why: e_∞ ≈ τ·b = 1 × 0.01 = 0.01 rad ≈ 0.57°. 34° is the unfiltered gyro after a minute (b·t), which the filter avoids.

q: Δt = 0.002 s, α = 0.995, gyro bias 0.01 rad/s. Roughly what steady error does the filter settle at?
choices: About 0.004 rad, a quarter of a degree
About 0.04 rad, over two degrees
About 0.00002 rad, effectively zero
About 0.025 rad, about 1.4 degrees
why: τ ≈ 0.4 s, so τ·b ≈ 0.004 rad ≈ 0.23°. 0.025 rad would be b/τ, the inverted relation.

q: Moving α closer to 1 (larger τ, lower f_c) does what?
choices: Lets less footfall through, but pays more bias error τ·b
Lets more footfall through, but pays less bias error τ·b
Lowers both the footfall leak and the bias error
Changes nothing on a walk; only the noise level matters
why: A lower f_c cuts more of the footfall band but trusts the gyro longer, so τ·b grows. That trade is why there is an optimum.

q: 'α is not a constant, it is a claim about your sensors.' A worse gyro bias pushes the best α toward…
choices: Smaller τ: α further from 1
Larger τ: α closer to 1
Exactly 0.998, whatever the sensors
α = 1, a pure gyro
why: The bias cost is τ·b, so a bigger b favours a shorter memory. A rougher gait does the opposite: it pushes toward larger τ.

q: A rougher gait (bigger footfall kicks) pushes the best filter time constant τ…
choices: Larger: lean longer on the gyro
Smaller: lean more on the accelerometer
To zero: use the accelerometer alone
Nowhere: τ depends only on Δt
why: Rougher footfalls make the accelerometer worse, so you trust it less, which means a lower f_c and a larger τ. A worse bias pushes the other way.

q: Where is the best α on the course's biased-gyro walk (Δt = 0.002 s)?
choices: About 0.998, τ ≈ 1 s
About 0.9, τ ≈ 0.02 s
About 0.995, τ ≈ 0.4 s
Exactly 1, a pure gyro
why: The sweep's optimum is around α ≈ 0.998 (mean and final error both bottom out there). 0.995 is the deck's default setting, not the optimum.

q: How much of the 0.77 Hz stride component of the accelerometer error gets through the low-pass at α = 0.995, and at α = 0.998?
choices: About 46 % and about 20 %
About 20 % and about 46 %
None at either, since the low-pass blocks it
All of it at 0.995, about 46 % at 0.998
why: At α = 0.995, f_c = 0.40 Hz sits too close to 0.77 Hz and almost half the stride error leaks; α = 0.998 (f_c 0.16 Hz) cuts it to 20 %, at the price of τ·b rising from 0.23° to 0.57°.

q: The gait's step time is 0.65 s and one stride is two steps. What is the stride frequency?
choices: About 0.77 Hz
About 1.54 Hz
About 0.65 Hz
About 0.33 Hz

q: Why does the complementary filter work at all?
choices: The two sensors' errors sit in different frequency bands
The two sensors' errors have opposite signs and cancel
The gyro's bias vanishes once the robot starts walking
The accelerometer's noise is filtered inside the chip
why: The gyro's error is the bias, at 0 Hz, removed by the high-pass; the accelerometer's is footfalls, from 0.77 Hz up, cut by the low-pass. Nothing cancels by sign.

q: On the biased-gyro walk, what were the MEAN errors of accelerometer only, gyro only, and the filter at α = 0.995?
why: Accelerometer ~6°, gyro 1.35°, filter 1.43°: the gyro's mean is slightly LOWER than the filter's. 21°, 2.5° and 1.02° are the worst/final-error numbers.

q: On the same walk, what were the FINAL errors?
choices: Accel ~4.5° (worst 21°); gyro 2.50° and growing; filter 1.02°
Accel ~1.02°; gyro 2.50° and growing; filter ~4.5° (worst 21°)
Accel ~4.5°; gyro 1.35° and steady; filter 1.43° and steady
Accel ~21°; gyro 0.57° and steady; filter 0.23° and steady
why: The filter ends lowest (1.02°); the gyro ends at 2.5×that and is still growing as b·t; the accelerometer is noisy, worst 21°.

q: On the walk, a student sets α = 0.90 'to trust the accelerometer more, since it never drifts'. Result?
choices: Footfalls leak straight through: several degrees of error
The best estimate of all, since drift is fully removed
Identical to α = 0.995, since the gyro bias is small
A pure gyro estimate that drifts away as b·t
why: At α = 0.90 (τ ≈ 0.02 s) the filter trusts the accelerometer too much, so every footfall kick appears as tilt, and the error is several degrees. Not drifting is not the same as being accurate.

q: 'Filtering more is always better, so push α all the way to 1.' Why is this wrong?
choices: At α = 1 the filter is a pure gyro and drifts as b·t
At α = 1 the filter is a pure accelerometer and is kicked
At α = 1 the filter divides by zero and cannot run
It is right: α = 1 gives the lowest error on any walk
why: α = 1 removes the accelerometer term entirely, so nothing corrects the gyro's bias and the error grows for ever. The optimum on the walk was about 0.998, not 1.

q: 'Over a long walk, a gyro's bias errors average out.' Is that right?
choices: No: a constant bias pushes one way, so e = b·t only grows
Yes: positive and negative bias cancel over many strides
Yes: the footfalls shake the bias out of the gyro
No: the error grows as ½·b·t², a parabola, for a gyro
why: A bias is a constant offset, so integration adds b·Δt with the same sign every step: 'drift only goes one way'. ½bt² is the double-integrated accelerometer, not the gyro.

q: Pure gyro: mean error 1.35°. Filter: 1.43°. For a robot that will run for an hour, which do you choose?
choices: The filter: the gyro's error keeps growing (final 2.5° vs 1.02°)
The gyro: its mean error is lower, so it is more accurate
Either: a 0.08° difference in mean error is negligible
The accelerometer: its error is the only one that never grows
why: Mean error is the wrong judge for a long run: the gyro starts exact and walks away as b·t, so its mean hides a final error that keeps growing. The accelerometer is bounded but ~6° on average.

q: With o = h(s) + noise, what does 'privileged' mean?
choices: In s, but not recoverable from any function of o
In o, but too noisy to use without a filter
Computable from o, but only through a filter
Measured by sensors that only the trainer owns
why: Observable = computable from o, perhaps through a filter (like tilt). Privileged = in the simulator state s but unrecoverable from o: world position, yaw, height above floor, contact forces, friction.

q: Which of these is OBSERVABLE on the G1?
choices: Gravity in the body frame, via IMU and filter
Body height above the floor, from qpos[2]
Heading (yaw) in the world, from the gyro
Foot contact forces, from the ankle motors
why: Roll/pitch (as the gravity direction) come from the IMU through a filter. Height has no sensor, yaw is blind to gravity and drifts on the gyro, and the G1 has no foot force sensors.

q: Which of these is PRIVILEGED on the G1?
choices: Foot contact forces
Joint velocities qvel[6:]
Angular velocity
The previous action
why: The G1 has no foot contact or force sensors. Joint velocities come from differentiated encoders, angular velocity from the gyro, and the previous action is what the robot itself commanded.

q: How does a real G1 obtain its joint velocities qvel[6:]?
choices: By differentiating the encoder angles
From the gyroscope's three axes
By integrating the accelerometer once
It can't: joint velocities are privileged
why: Encoders give angles; their rate of change is the joint velocity, so it is observable. The gyro measures the body's turning rate, not individual joints.

q: Why may a policy include its previous action in its observation?
choices: The robot commanded it, so it knows it exactly
The IMU measures it through the motors' reaction
The encoders record it at the physics rate
It is privileged, but allowed because it is small
why: Nothing needs to be sensed: the controller itself sent that command, so it is genuinely known on hardware.

q: Why is world position qpos[:2] excluded from the observation?
choices: No sensor sees it, and double integration diverges
It is too large a number for the network to use
The encoders measure it, but only at 50 Hz
It is observable, but redundant with the yaw
why: Position needs a sensor that sees the world; the IMU route grows as ½bt². So it is privileged, and a policy trained on it could not leave the simulator.

q: Gravity in body frame + gyro + all joint angles + all joint velocities: how many numbers, all measurable?
why: 3 + 3 + 29 + 29 = 64. 42 is week 7's leg-only input; 71 = 36 + 35 is the full qpos + qvel state.

q: Week 7's leg-only walking environment: how many inputs and outputs?
choices: 42 in, 12 leg targets out
64 in, 29 joint targets out
36 in (qpos), 29 targets out
42 in, 29 joint targets out
why: Gravity 3 + angular velocity 3 + 12 leg angles + 12 leg velocities + the previous 12-number action = 42 in, and 12 leg targets out.

q: How large is the G1's full simulator state s, counting qpos and qvel?
choices: 36 + 35 numbers, plus contacts, friction, terrain, masses
29 + 29 numbers, one angle and one rate per actuator only
7 + 6 numbers, just the floating base pose and its twist
64 + 42 numbers, the two observation vectors put together
why: qpos has 36 numbers (7 free-joint + 29 hinges) and qvel 35 (6 + 29). The state also includes contacts, friction, terrain and masses, none of which the robot measures.

q: In asymmetric actor-critic, which network sees what?
choices: The actor sees only o; the critic may see all of s
The actor sees all of s; the critic sees only o
Both see only o, since both are deployed
Both see all of s; only the actor is trained
why: The actor (policy) runs on the robot, so it may use only what the robot measures. The critic (value function) is used only in training and then thrown away, so it may use privileged state.

q: Why may the critic in asymmetric actor-critic use privileged information?
choices: It is used only during training, then discarded
It runs on the robot's computer, which holds s
Its inputs are filtered, which makes them observable
It only scores falls, which the robot can sense
why: Privileged information is used where it is legal: in simulation, during training. Its better view makes its scores more accurate, which helps the actor learn; the deployed actor stays honest.

q: To score a tilt filter on the walking G1, what should the 'true' orientation be?
choices: The IMU site's own orientation, which differs from the pelvis by up to 0.7°
The pelvis orientation from qpos[3:7], since the IMU is bolted near it
The accelerometer tilt measured at rest, before the walk begins
The bias-free gyro integral, since a perfect gyro is nearly exact
why: The torso IMU and the pelvis are different bodies; while walking they differ by up to 0.7°, which is the size of the filter errors themselves. Scoring against the pelvis would hide or invent errors.

q: While walking, how much do the torso IMU site's orientation and the pelvis orientation differ?
choices: Up to about 0.7°, the size of the filter errors
Up to about 7°, far above the filter errors
Up to about 0.007°, negligible for scoring
Exactly 0°: the two are rigidly joined
why: They differ by up to 0.7° (the waist joints sit between them), as big as the 1.02°–1.43° filter errors being measured. That is why the truth must come from site_xmat of the IMU site.
